title: 140. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Relative Motion with Constant Speeds
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the relative speed of two objects moving in the same direction.
questions.question: Car A travels at \(60\text{ km/h}\) and Car B travels in the same direction at \(40\text{ km/h}\). What is the relative speed of Car A with respect to Car B?
questions.explanation: For same-direction motion, the relative speed is the difference of the speeds. Here, \(60-40=20\). Therefore, the relative speed is \(20\text{ km/h}\). Option B incorrectly adds the speeds.
questions.hint: Determine whether the objects move in the same or opposite directions.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the relative speed of two objects moving toward each other.
questions.question: Two trains approach each other at \(50\text{ km/h}\) and \(70\text{ km/h}\). What is their relative speed?
questions.explanation: For opposite-direction motion, the relative speed is the sum of the speeds. Here, \(50+70=120\). Therefore, the relative speed is \(120\text{ km/h}\). Option B incorrectly subtracts the speeds.
questions.hint: Track the rate at which the separation changes.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the time for two objects moving toward each other to meet.
questions.question: Two towns are \(180\text{ km}\) apart. Two cars start at the same time from the two towns and travel toward each other at \(40\text{ km/h}\) and \(50\text{ km/h}\). How long will it take for them to meet?
questions.explanation: The combined speed is \(40+50=90\text{ km/h}\). The time to meet is \(\frac{180}{90}=2\text{ h}\). Therefore, they meet after \(2\text{ h}\). The alternative ignores one approaching car and uses \(\frac{180}{40}=4.5\text{ h}\).
questions.hint: Identify the gap or combined length that the relative motion must cover.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the time for a faster object to catch a slower object.
questions.question: Cyclist A rides at \(15\text{ km/h}\), and Cyclist B rides ahead in the same direction at \(10\text{ km/h}\). If Cyclist A is \(20\text{ km}\) behind Cyclist B, how long will it take Cyclist A to catch Cyclist B?
questions.explanation: The relative speed is \(15-10=5\text{ km/h}\). The time to close the \(20\text{ km}\) gap is \(\frac{20}{5}=4\text{ h}\). Therefore, Cyclist A catches Cyclist B after \(4\text{ h}\). The alternative adds same-direction speeds, using \(\frac{20}{15+10}=0.8\text{ h}\) instead of the closing-speed difference.
questions.hint: Determine whether the objects move in the same or opposite directions.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the time after the faster object starts to catch the slower object.
questions.question: Runner A leaves a point at \(08{:}00\) traveling at \(6\text{ km/h}\). Runner B leaves the same point at \(09{:}00\) traveling at \(8\text{ km/h}\) along the same route. How long after \(09{:}00\) does Runner B catch Runner A?
questions.explanation: By \(09{:}00\), Runner A has traveled \(6\text{ km}\). The relative speed is \(8-6=2\text{ km/h}\). The time to close the \(6\text{ km}\) gap is \(\frac{6}{2}=3\text{ h}\) after \(09{:}00\). Therefore, Runner B catches Runner A after \(3\text{ h}\). The alternative reports \(4\text{ h}\) from the earlier \(08{:}00\) departure rather than \(3\text{ h}\) after \(09{:}00\).
questions.hint: Track the rate at which the separation changes.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the relative speed of two objects moving in opposite directions.
questions.question: Two objects move in opposite directions at \(3\text{ m/s}\) and \(5\text{ m/s}\). What is their relative speed?
questions.explanation: For opposite-direction motion, the relative speed is the sum of the speeds. Here, \(3+5=8\). Therefore, the relative speed is \(8\text{ m/s}\). Option B incorrectly subtracts the speeds.
questions.hint: Determine whether the objects move in the same or opposite directions.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the relative speed of two objects moving in the same direction.
questions.question: Two objects move in the same direction at \(12\text{ m/s}\) and \(20\text{ m/s}\). What is their relative speed?
questions.explanation: For same-direction motion, the relative speed is the difference of the speeds. Here, \(20-12=8\). Therefore, the relative speed is \(8\text{ m/s}\). Option A incorrectly adds the speeds.
questions.hint: Determine whether the objects move in the same or opposite directions.

questions.concept: Meeting Time on a Circular Track in Opposite Directions
questions.learningObjective: Determine the time for two objects on a circular track to meet again.
questions.question: Two runners start from the same point on a \(400\text{ m}\) circular track at the same time and run in opposite directions at \(6\text{ m/s}\) and \(4\text{ m/s}\). How long until they meet again?
questions.explanation: Because they run in opposite directions, their speeds add. The combined speed is \(6+4=10\text{ m/s}\). They meet again after together covering one full lap: \(\frac{400}{10}=40\text{ s}\). Therefore, they meet again after \(40\text{ s}\). The alternative ignores the second runner, using \(\frac{400}{6}\approx 66.7\text{ s}\).
questions.hint: Track the rate at which the separation changes.

questions.concept: Catch-Up Time on a Circular Track in the Same Direction
questions.learningObjective: Determine the time for a faster runner to catch a slower runner on a circular track.
questions.question: Two runners start from the same point on a \(400\text{ m}\) circular track at the same time and run in the same direction at \(5\text{ m/s}\) and \(3\text{ m/s}\). How long until the faster runner catches the slower runner?
questions.explanation: For same-direction motion on a circular track, the faster runner must gain one full lap on the slower runner. The relative speed is \(5-3=2\text{ m/s}\). The time is \(\frac{400}{2}=200\text{ s}\). Therefore, the faster runner catches the slower runner after \(200\text{ s}\). The alternative adds the same-direction speeds, \(\frac{400}{5+3}=50\text{ s}\), instead of using their difference.
questions.hint: Identify the gap or combined length that the relative motion must cover.

questions.concept: Time for Two Moving Trains to Pass Each Other
questions.learningObjective: Determine the time for two trains moving in opposite directions to completely pass each other.
questions.question: Train A is \(200\text{ m}\) long and travels at \(20\text{ m/s}\). Train B is \(300\text{ m}\) long and travels in the opposite direction at \(10\text{ m/s}\). How long does it take from the moment they first meet until they have completely passed each other? Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: When two trains pass each other in opposite directions, the total distance to be covered is the sum of their lengths: \(200+300=500\text{ m}\). The relative speed is \(20+10=30\text{ m/s}\). The time is \(\frac{500}{30}\approx 16.7\text{ s}\). Therefore, the trains completely pass each other after about \(16.7\text{ s}\). The alternative ignores Train B's motion, using \(\frac{500}{20}=25\text{ s}\) instead of dividing by the relative speed.
questions.hint: Determine whether the objects move in the same or opposite directions.
